title: Database Transaction Isolation and Atomicity
statement: Which ACID property guarantees that once a transaction has committed, its changes survive system crashes and power failures?
explanation: Durability guarantees that once a transaction has been committed, it will remain committed even in the case of a system crash, usually implemented via Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) to non-volatile storage.

title: Boyce-Codd Normal Form Definition
statement: A relation schema R is in Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) if for every non-trivial functional dependency X -> Y:

options.text: X is a Candidate Key and Y is non-prime

explanation: BCNF requires that for every non-trivial functional dependency X -> Y, X must be a superkey of relation R. 3NF allows Y to be a prime attribute, but BCNF strictly eliminates this exception.

title: B+ Tree vs B Tree Storage in Relational Databases
statement: Why are B+ Trees preferred over standard B-Trees for database disk indexes?

options.text: B+ Trees have fewer levels and all actual data records are stored exclusively in linked leaf nodes for fast range scans
B+ Trees store data in internal nodes only
B+ Trees do not require rebalancing on insertion
B+ Trees have O(1) worst-case search complexity

explanation: In a B+ tree, internal nodes store only routing keys (allowing higher fanout and shallower tree height), while all data pointers reside in leaf nodes, which are linked together in a doubly linked list for optimal sequential and range queries.

title: HAVING vs WHERE Clause in SQL
statement: In SQL, what is the key difference between the WHERE clause and the HAVING clause?

options.text: WHERE filters rows before aggregation; HAVING filters grouped rows after aggregation with functions like SUM/COUNT
WHERE is used with aggregate functions; HAVING is used with individual row columns
WHERE and HAVING can be used interchangeably in any SQL statement
HAVING is executed before GROUP BY

explanation: WHERE filters individual records prior to grouping. HAVING is applied after GROUP BY to filter aggregate results (e.g. HAVING COUNT(*) > 5).
